lessonTitle: Cardiac and Gut Development: Origins of Common Defects

blocks.text: A newborn born at 29 weeks needs ventilator support, and on day four a doctor hears a continuous murmur below the left clavicle. A vessel that was essential before birth has failed to close. Understanding how the heart and gut are built from simple tubes explains why such defects arise and where they sit.

blocks.markdown: The heart forms from a single tube that loops, then is divided into four chambers by **septa**. The atria are separated by two overlapping septa: the **septum primum** grows down from the roof and leaves the **ostium primum** beneath it; before that closes, apoptosis opens the **ostium secundum** in the septum primum. The thicker **septum secundum** grows beside it and leaves the **foramen ovale**, so blood still passes right to left through the foramen ovale before birth. The ventricles are divided by a muscular interventricular septum growing up from the floor and a **membranous septum** that closes the gap at the top, formed from endocardial cushion tissue and the aorticopulmonary septum.

blocks.title: Septal defect
blocks.text: A persistent opening between the left and right sides of the heart caused by failure of a septum to form, grow or fuse. Defects are named by the chamber and the part of the septum involved: atrial septal defect (ASD) and ventricular septal defect (VSD).

rows: ASD secundum (most common)
Excessive resorption of septum primum or deficient septum secundum, leaving a large opening at the fossa ovalis
Left-to-right shunt at atrial level
ASD primum
Septum primum does not fuse with the endocardial cushions, so ostium primum persists
Low in the septum; may involve the atrioventricular valves
Patent foramen ovale
Septum primum and secundum fail to fuse after birth
Often silent; flap valve opens if right atrial pressure exceeds left
VSD, membranous (most common)
Failure of the membranous septum to close
Left-to-right shunt through the upper septum
VSD, muscular
Defect in the muscular septum
May lie anywhere in the muscular part
blocks.caption: Septal defects and their embryological origin.

blocks.markdown: Before birth the lungs are fluid-filled and pulmonary vascular resistance is high, so three shunts bypass them: the **ductus venosus** (umbilical vein blood past the liver), the **foramen ovale** (right atrium to left atrium) and the **ductus arteriosus** (pulmonary trunk to the aorta, joining just beyond the left subclavian artery). At birth, lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance and raises oxygen tension; the ductus arteriosus constricts within hours to days and later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. If it fails to close, it remains a **patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)**. As pulmonary resistance falls, blood flows from the higher-pressure aorta to the pulmonary trunk, a left-to-right shunt, producing a continuous murmur. Prematurity is a major risk factor because the ductus is less responsive to the stimuli for closure.
In a left-to-right shunt the pulmonary blood flow ($Q_p$) exceeds the systemic flow ($Q_s$). The extra flow is the shunt flow:

blocks.caption: Left-to-right shunt flow and pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (flows in L/min).

blocks.title: Quantifying a shunt
blocks.prompt: A child with a VSD has pulmonary blood flow 8.0 L/min and systemic blood flow 5.0 L/min. Find the shunt flow and the flow ratio.

steps.text: Shunt flow is the excess over systemic flow.

blocks.markdown: The gut develops from the foregut, midgut and hindgut. The midgut grows faster than the abdominal cavity, so in the sixth week it herniates into the umbilical cord around the **superior mesenteric artery** axis. During herniation it rotates 90 degrees anticlockwise (viewed from the front); when it returns at about week ten it rotates a further 180 degrees, a total of 270 degrees, which places the duodenojejunal junction to the left, the caecum in the right iliac fossa and fixes the colon in its normal position.

rows: Malrotation
Incomplete rotation; the gut is not fixed normally
Risk of volvulus around the superior mesenteric artery, causing obstruction and ischaemia
Omphalocele
Midgut fails to return to the abdomen
Defect at the umbilicus, covered by a membrane
Gastroschisis
Abdominal wall defect, usually to the right of the umbilicus
Exposed bowel without a covering membrane
Meckel's diverticulum
Persistence of the vitelline (vitello-intestinal) duct
Pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum
Duodenal atresia
Failure of recanalisation of the duodenal lumen
Bilious vomiting in the newborn, associated with Down syndrome
blocks.caption: Common gut malformations and their embryological origin.

blocks.title: Rotation of the midgut
blocks.prompt: Show how the normal total rotation of the midgut arises, and state what is predicted if the second step fails.

steps.text: The midgut rotates 90 degrees anticlockwise during herniation into the cord.
It rotates a further 180 degrees as it returns to the abdomen.
If the second rotation fails the gut is malrotated and the loop is not properly fixed; a narrow mesenteric base allows twisting around the superior mesenteric artery (volvulus).

blocks.answer: Normal total rotation is 270 degrees; failure of the return rotation causes malrotation with risk of volvulus.

blocks.title: From embryology to the lesion
blocks.text: Ask which step failed: growth, fusion, rotation, recanalisation or closure. The step tells you where the defect lies and why the symptoms follow, for example a left-to-right shunt after pulmonary resistance falls.

blocks.title: Do not confuse omphalocele with gastroschisis
blocks.text: An omphalocele is a midline defect with a covering sac and often accompanies other anomalies, whereas gastroschisis is a defect beside the umbilicus with exposed bowel and no sac.

points: Atrial defects arise from failure of the septum primum or secundum to form or fuse; membranous VSD arises from failure of the membranous septum to close.
The ductus arteriosus normally closes soon after birth and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum; persistence leaves a patent ductus and a left-to-right shunt.
Midgut rotates 270 degrees in total; failure of return or rotation causes omphalocele, malrotation and volvulus, and persistent vitelline duct causes Meckel's diverticulum.

questions.stem: An infant has an ASD at the site of the fossa ovalis, caused by excessive resorption of the septum primum. Which defect is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: an enlarged ostium secundum from excessive resorption of the septum primum gives a secundum ASD.
distractorRationale.b: The ostium primum defect arises when the septum primum fails to fuse with the cushions.
distractorRationale.d: PDA is a vascular channel, not a septal defect.

questions.explanation: A secundum ASD results from a large opening in the septum primum or a deficient septum secundum. A primum ASD instead lies low in the septum because the septum primum fails to meet the endocardial cushions.

questions.stem: Which structure's failure to develop correctly results in the most common type of VSD?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the membranous septum is the most common site of VSD.
distractorRationale.c: The foramen ovale flap is atrial.
distractorRationale.d: The tricuspid valve is not a septum.

questions.explanation: The membranous interventricular septum is formed from endocardial cushion tissue and aorticopulmonary septal tissue, and failure of closure leaves the commonest VSD. The muscular septum is a less common site.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the ductus arteriosus?

options.text: A fetal vessel linking the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, normally becoming the ligamentum arteriosum
A fetal vessel linking the right atrium to the left atrium
A fetal vessel linking the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava
A vessel linking the left atrium to the left ventricle

questions.correctOptionText: A fetal vessel linking the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, normally becoming the ligamentum arteriosum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
distractorRationale.d: This is the mitral valve region, not a fetal shunt.

questions.explanation: The ductus arteriosus carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs. Closure at birth leaves the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old girl has a continuous machinery murmur at the left upper sternal border and bounding pulses. The most probable explanation is:

options.text: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close, producing a left-to-right shunt
Failure of the ductus venosus to open

questions.correctOptionText: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close, producing a left-to-right shunt

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a PDA gives a continuous murmur and left-to-right shunt.
distractorRationale.b: The ductus venosus is part of fetal circulation of the liver, not a cause of murmur.
distractorRationale.c: Midgut rotation affects the gut, not the heart.
distractorRationale.d: Vitelline duct persistence causes Meckel's diverticulum.

questions.explanation: After birth pulmonary resistance falls and the aorta pressure exceeds that of the pulmonary trunk, so blood flows through a persistent ductus into the pulmonary circulation, causing a continuous murmur. Prematurity predisposes because the ductus responds poorly to the closure stimuli.

questions.stem: A baby with a PDA has pulmonary blood flow 9.0 L/min and systemic blood flow 6.0 L/min. Calculate the left-to-right shunt flow in L/min using $Q_{shunt} = Q_p - Q_s$.
questions.explanation: Shunt flow equals the difference between pulmonary and systemic flow, 9.0 minus 6.0 = 3.0 L/min. The extra blood recirculates through the lungs without supplying the body.

questions.stem: A patient has a left-to-right shunt. Pulmonary blood flow is 10.0 L/min and systemic blood flow is 6.5 L/min. What percentage of pulmonary blood flow is shunted blood?
questions.explanation: Shunt flow is 10.0 minus 6.5 = 3.5 L/min. As a fraction of pulmonary flow this is 3.5/10.0 = 0.35, or 35%.

questions.stem: A newborn has loops of bowel outside the abdomen, covered by a thin membranous sac, at the umbilicus. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: The midgut failed to return to the abdominal cavity after physiological herniation
The vitelline duct persisted as a diverticulum
The dorsal bud of the pancreas failed to form

questions.correctOptionText: The midgut failed to return to the abdominal cavity after physiological herniation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: omphalocele is failure of return of the midgut.
distractorRationale.b: A persistent vitelline duct gives a diverticulum, not an external sac.
distractorRationale.d: The ductus arteriosus is a cardiac vessel.

questions.explanation: The midgut herniates into the cord and should return by week ten. If it does not, bowel remains in a membranous sac at the umbilicus, an omphalocele.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old has painless rectal bleeding. Imaging shows a pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. This is a remnant of which embryonic structure?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Meckel's diverticulum is a vitelline duct remnant.
distractorRationale.b: The ductus venosus is a hepatic vascular shunt.
distractorRationale.d: The allantois relates to the urachus, not the ileum.

questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the vitello-intestinal duct located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. It illustrates failure of an embryonic duct to obliterate.

questions.stem: Explain how a failure of fusion of the septum primum with the endocardial cushions produces an ASD, and name the type of defect.
markingGuide: Septum primum normally grows down to meet the endocardial cushions.
Failure to fuse leaves the ostium primum open.
The defect is an ostium primum ASD, low in the septum.
Blood shunts left to right between the atria.
questions.explanation: The ostium primum is the gap beneath the septum primum. If the septum does not meet the cushions the gap persists and forms a primum ASD, allowing blood to shunt from the higher-pressure left atrium to the right.

questions.stem: Describe the normal rotation of the midgut and explain how malrotation can lead to a volvulus.
markingGuide: Midgut herniates into the umbilical cord and rotates 90 degrees anticlockwise around the SMA.
On return it rotates a further 180 degrees, 270 degrees in total.
Normal fixation of the colon and mesentery gives a broad base.
Malrotation leaves a narrow mesenteric base.
The narrow base allows twisting around the superior mesenteric artery, causing obstruction and ischaemia.
questions.explanation: A normally rotated gut is fixed over a broad mesenteric attachment, so it cannot twist. When rotation fails, the narrow stalk centred on the superior mesenteric artery allows the loop to twist, obstructing the lumen and compromising blood supply.
